children: 1845 ET - Japanese stocks may remain rangebound amid caution over the U.S. midterm elections and continued uncertainty over the Middle East conflict. Nikkei futures open at 63425, up 1210 points from Tuesday and up 245 points from Monday, on the SGX. Japanese markets were closed Tuesday for a national holiday. The dollar is at 158.65 yen, compared with Y157.88 as of Monday's Tokyo stock market close. Investors are focusing on U.S. election results as well as domestic earnings. The Nikkei Stock Average fell 0.3% to 63081.86 on Monday. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com)

1449 ET - Purchasing managers indexes for Mexico were mixed in October, while hovering around the 50 threshold between expansion and contraction. The IMEF manufacturing index edges up to 49.8 from 49.7, the Bank of Mexico/Inegi index rises 1.2 points to 50.5 and the S&P Global index falls to 49.5 from 50.3 in September. "The manufacturing sector continues to show signs of stabilization, supported by a recovery in demand and employment, although there are still differences among its components that limit the strength of the advance," IMEF says. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1400 ET - Mexico received $5.36 billion in remittances in September, up 1.6% from the year-earlier month, the Bank of Mexico reports. The increase followed a 3.6% year-on-year decline in August and brought remittances for the first nine months of the year to $47.16 billion, up 2.1% from the first nine months of 2025. Attention in 4Q will focus on performance in the U.S. agricultural and construction sectors, analysts at Grupo Financiero Banorte say in a note. "Headwinds in sectors that traditionally employ Mexican migrants could weigh on inflows toward the end of the year." Raids and deportations of migrants have restricted labor supply, including effects on absenteeism, while cyclical factors including adverse weather and a sluggish housing sector could pressure activity and have an impact on labor demand, they say. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1344 ET - Goods exports from Latin America and the Caribbean rose 19.5% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, the Inter-American Development Bank says. The bank's Trade and Integration Monitor 2026 shows that export growth outpacing the 14.5% increase in overall world trade. Growth was driven by higher prices for oil and other commodities and also by demand for infrastructure associated with artificial intelligence, the bank adds. The share of U.S. imports from Latin America and the Caribbean hit a record high of 22.1% in the first half of this year, while U.S. purchases from the rest of the world declined, the bank says. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)

1336 ET - The heist that pulled billions in digital currencies off of crypto exchange Binance wasn't the result of a single compromised laptop, Binance co-CEO Richard Teng tells CNBC. "This is not one single mistake or one click," he says. The attackers, believed to be linked to North Korea, built a fake developer tool and lured a Binance engineer to download it, Teng says. They also used fake job interviews to install malware on employees' devices. From there, they were able to gain access to the system that authorizes wallet transactions, Teng says, noting that the entire process took months. "We are letting the world know, we are pushing for real transparency, because we need to learn together on that front and we need to continue to improve the security as an industry," he says.(elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1333 ET - Binance co-CEO Richard Teng says the cryptocurrency company is responsible for a breach that let hackers take $6.3 billion from digital wallets on its exchange. "This shouldn't have happened," Teng says on CNBC. "We take full responsibility on that front." He adds that while an internal AI tool was used by the hackers to carry out the heist, AI models also serve as the best line of defense against cyberattacks. Asked why users should continue to trust Binance, he says that the company has closed entry points used by the hackers, rebuilt compromised tools and systems, and scanned its employees' devices. The company has commissioned an independent expert review. "We have done everything we can," he says.  (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1229 ET - A relatively animated Tiff Macklem, the Bank of Canada governor, defends his decision to raise the policy rate last week upon questioning from Canadian lawmakers. A lawmaker from the governing Liberals says the rate hike could dampen efforts by PM Mark Carney to encourage increased business investment. Macklem acknowledges that tighter financial conditions might dampen investment enthusiasm. However, rate policy is the most important tool the BOC has to control inflation, and failing to raise rates runs the risk that "the prices of everything will be going up." The BOC's No. 2 official, Carolyn Rogers, adds lower rates might help on balance in spurring investment, "but not if it comes with increasing inflation." (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1225 ET - Brazil's central bank is expected to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 13.75% tomorrow, Natixis's Benito Berber says in a note. That would interrupt an easing cycle and keep borrowing costs among the highest in the world. Investors are worried about rising government spending after the reelection of Lula da Silva last month. Berber expects rates to be on hold "until the government provides clearer signals on its fiscal plans." Lula is in the process of choosing a new finance minister, while inflation expectations have risen. The Brazilian real weakens 1% against the dollar. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1217 ET - The job openings report for September came in hotter than expected with a four-month high, BMO analysts say in a research note. That provides a solid read on labor demand that reinforces the Fed's hawkish bias and supports the base-case expectation for a quarter-point rate increase at the FOMC's December meeting, the analysts say. The Treasury market has sold off to session lows since the data came out, they say. The 10-year yield has floated around 5% as an equilibrium, and will probably continue to do so as the market digests the midterm election results, among other headlines, the analysts say. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1148 ET - Canada may not have seen sweeping layoffs in the wake of the Trump administration's tariffs but employers appear to be absorbing the pressures, according to a survey by labor law firm Littler. The latest changes to U.S. Section 339 tariffs are now in effect, shuffling the goods facing 50% levies. Littler says that beyond pausing hiring and cutting jobs, 24% of surveyed Canadian employers restructured or redeployed staff and 23% delayed raises or bonuses. And 19% have offered voluntary exits or buyouts and 16% reduced hours outside the federal Work-Sharing Program. Littler said among employers that took workforce actions like these, 83% said U.S. tariff disruptions contributed. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

1138 ET - Bank of Canada Gov. Tiff Macklem tells lawmakers that the Canadian economy is showing "impressive resilience," and as a result rate policy no longer needs to be as accommodative. Macklem adds that, even with last week's quarter-point hike to 2.5%, rate policy "is still not restraining growth. We've actually been supporting growth, but the economy doesn't need quite as much support." The BOC estimates the neutral rate of interest — whereby policy neither stimulates nor hinders activity — to be in the 2.25% to 3.25% range. The rate hike, he says, reflects the buildup of cost pressures, and the expectation that an increasing share of firms intend to pass on those expenses through higher prices. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1137 ET - The backdrop for global fixed income has changed meaningfully, with bonds repriced reflecting persistent inflation and elevated government borrowing, Payden & Rygel's Eric Souders says in a note. "Yields have moved higher as investors contend with persistent inflation, elevated government borrowing, and uncertainty around the path for interest rates," the director and portfolio manager says. "But that repricing has also created a more attractive starting point for bond investors." Higher starting yields provide greater income and a larger cushion against further increases in rates, while a still-resilient global economy continues to create opportunities across credit markets, he says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)
